scenario: AITA for displaying my students’ memes in front of the class? | I teach high school juniors and seniors. This happened a few months ago so it’s pretty inconsequential now, but I’m curious. I sent out a class email with a homework assignment and made a misspelling. Some of my students decided to turn that misspelling into a dumb meme and post it on our class discussions page... without realizing I could see it. It got a little crude but nothing out of the ordinary for 18 year olds and nothing was directed at anyone in particular. I honestly found it kind of funny that they were making fun of me and my class (and other things, the meme ended up including things like Harry Potter jokes and the like) without realizing I could also see it. I decided to address the issue that I would start that class by putting some screenshots of those memes on the projector. I said something along the lines of “I’m glad you all have finally utilized the class discussions feature, these are some interesting points that we can discuss now.” Of course they got embarrassed and we moved on. All the major meme makers apologized after but I told them it was no big deal and made sure to laugh it off so they didn’t think they were actually in trouble. I told this story to my brother who is also a teacher and he accused me of public shaming and said that it was a terrible teaching method and that my students are probably still cut up about it. I mostly just thought the incident was harmless and funny but now I’m unsure. Was I an asshole for doing what I did?

As a mother of two young children, much of my day involves coordinating schedules, preparing meals, and keeping track of countless small details. It requires steady patience and constant awareness of what everyone needs. Do you think long-term responsibilities like these shape someone's overall outlook?

Absolutely—those day‑to‑day responsibilities can have a profound, lasting impact on how you see the world and how you approach life’s challenges. ### 1. **A Built‑In Habit of Anticipation** When you’re constantly juggling schedules, you’re always thinking ahead. That habit of planning and foreseeing potential hiccups can spill over into other areas—career decisions, financial planning, even personal relationships. Over time, you develop a “future‑oriented” mindset that can help you spot opportunities and mitigate risks before they become problems. ### 2. **Resilience Through Repetition** Every time a meal plan falls apart, a schedule gets bumped, or a child’s mood swings, you’re forced to adapt quickly. Repeated exposure to small crises builds a kind of “stress inoculation.” You learn to stay calm, find creative solutions, and bounce back. That resilience can translate into a more optimistic outlook on life’s bigger uncertainties. ### 3. **Empathy and Perspective** Caring for others—especially children—naturally expands your empathy. You become attuned to subtle cues, needs, and emotions that you might otherwise overlook. Over time, this heightened sensitivity can make you more compassionate in your professional life, in friendships, and even in your own self‑care. ### 4. **Prioritization and Value Clarification** Deciding what to cook, what to schedule, and what to let go of forces you to clarify what truly matters. You learn to weigh options quickly and make trade‑offs. This skill can help you set long‑term goals that align with your core values, rather than getting lost in the noise of everyday demands. ### 5. **Time‑Management as a Life Skill** The “time‑boxing” you use for meals and appointments becomes a framework for any project. You’re likely to be more efficient, set realistic deadlines, and avoid procrastination.
